pos: n. (a worker in copper or brass; the trade of Alexander, who withstood Paul)
etymology: From copper and smith. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's last letter, naming both the man and his trade: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil.
biblical_def: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words. Paul is writing from a Roman prison near the end of his life, and the passage around this verse is the most personal in his letters. Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world. Only Luke is with me. Bring the cloke that I left at Troas, and the books, but especially the parchments. And then Alexander, named with his trade so Timothy will know exactly which man to avoid. Paul does not take the reckoning into his own hands: the Lord reward him according to his works is a committal, not a curse pronounced by Paul's authority, and it matches his own rule in Romans to give place unto wrath. What follows is the more remarkable half. At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge. He asks judgment for the opposer and forgiveness for the deserters, and then says the thing that steadied him: notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils; in Scripture, the trade of Alexander, who greatly withstood Paul's words.
webster_full: COPPERSMITH, n. One whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils.
SMITH, n. Literally, the striker, the beater; hence, one who works in metals.
WITHSTAND, v.t. To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.
FORSAKE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from.
RECOMPENSE, n. An equivalent returned for anything given, done or suffered.
scriptures: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works:
Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words.
At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.
Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
corruption_summary: Naming an opposer by name is treated as unloving, so that churches are left unwarned; Paul names Alexander and his trade in an inspired letter and tells Timothy plainly to beware of him.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a widespread conviction that Christian charity forbids identifying a particular man as dangerous. The Pastorals do it repeatedly: Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul delivered unto Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme; Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection is past already and overthrew the faith of some; Demas, who forsook him; and here Alexander the coppersmith, identified by trade so there could be no mistake. The purpose is protective. A warning that cannot name anyone protects no one, and the shepherd's duty includes the wolves.

What keeps this from becoming a licence for personal feuding is the way Paul does it. He states the injury factually, hands the recompense to God rather than pursuing it himself, gives Timothy a practical instruction, and in the very next sentence prays that the men who abandoned him at his trial would not be charged with it. The dictionary takes that as the pattern: name what must be named, for the protection of the flock; leave vengeance to the Lord; and forgive the weak, who are not the same as the hostile.
roots_summary: Greek chalkeus (G5471), a worker in copper or brass; anthistemi (G436), to withstand or oppose; apodidomi (G591), to render or repay.
roots_lines: Greek chalkeus (G5471) — a worker in copper or brass; the one occurrence, 2 Timothy 4:14.
Greek anthistemi (G436) — to set oneself against, to withstand; he hath greatly withstood our words.
Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to recompense; the Lord reward him according to his works.
Greek enkataleipo (G1459) — to abandon, to forsake utterly; all men forsook me.

“I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge” — the deserters forgiven.
“the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me” — what remained when men did not.

pos: n. pl. (travelling traders; merchants who buy and sell)
etymology: Old English ceapman, from ceap, trade or bargain — the root also of cheap and of place names ending in -chipping. The Authorized Version uses it once, among the sources of Solomon's revenue.
biblical_def: Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon. The verse sits inside a chapter cataloguing a wealth that is hard to take in: six hundred threescore and six talents of gold in one year, targets and shields of beaten gold, a great ivory throne overlaid with pure gold with twelve lions upon the six steps, and silver in Jerusalem as stones. And the Chronicler gives the assessment plainly: king Solomon passed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, and all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, that God had put in his heart. The last clause is the one that governs the chapter. The wisdom was put there, and the queen of Sheba came a very long way to hear it and went home saying the half had not been told her. The Lord took that visit up as a witness against his own generation: the queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it, for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a cheapener; one that offers as a purchaser; a pedlar or itinerant trader.
webster_full: CHAPMAN, n. A cheapener; one that offers as a purchaser.
CHAPMAN, n. A man that buys and sells; an itinerant trader; a pedlar.
MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries.
TRAFFICK, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property.
scriptures: Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
And king Solomon passed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, that God had put in his heart.

The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.
corruption_summary: Wisdom is treated as a resource a man develops rather than a gift God puts in the heart, so that the Chronicler's own explanation of Solomon is set aside; and the greater than Solomon is left unmentioned.
corruption_paragraphs: The Chronicler will not let the reader admire Solomon on Solomon's account. The wisdom is that God had put in his heart, and the source was recorded long before in the dream at Gibeon, where a young king asked for an understanding heart to judge a great people and God gave him that and the riches he had not asked for. Every modern treatment of wisdom as a competence to be cultivated runs past this. James keeps the biblical order: if any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

The second thing the chapter is for is comparison, and the Lord made it himself. The queen of the south crossed a desert to hear a man; a greater than Solomon stood in Galilee teaching for nothing, and the generation that heard him asked for a sign. That is the sting of Matthew 12:42, and it is aimed at the well-supplied and the religiously informed rather than at the ignorant. The dictionary keeps it where the Lord put it: as a warning to those with the greatest access and the least hunger.
roots_summary: Hebrew tuwr (H8446), to travel about, to search out, and so a travelling trader; cachar (H5503), to trade or traffic; chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew tuwr (H8446) — to go about, to explore, to traffic; the chapmen of 2 Chronicles 9:14.
Hebrew cachar (H5503) — to travel as a trader, to traffic; the merchants beside them.

Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, to put, to set; that God had put in his heart.
Hebrew 'osher (H6239) — riches, wealth; he passed all the kings of the earth in riches.

“that God had put in his heart” — where the wisdom came from.
“a greater than Solomon is here” — the comparison the Lord drew.

pos: n. pl. (makers of perfumes and sweetmeats; among the trades a king will conscript)
etymology: From Latin conficere, to prepare or make up — one who compounds spices, ointments, and sweets. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Samuel's warning about the king Israel demanded.
biblical_def: And he will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers. Samuel is reading Israel the invoice before they sign. This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them for himself, for his chariots and to be his horsemen; he will set them to ear his ground and to reap his harvest; he will take your daughters; he will take your fields and your vineyards and your oliveyards, even the best of them; he will take the tenth of your seed and of your sheep; and ye shall be his servants. The verb take falls six times in eight verses. And the warning ends where every such warning ends: ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the LORD will not hear you in that day. The deepest note in the chapter, though, is God's own: they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. Israel wanted a king like all the nations, and God gave them exactly what they asked for, which is one of the more terrible forms his judgments take.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to make confections, comfits, or sweetmeats; in Scripture, one of the trades a king will conscript daughters into.
webster_full: CONFECTIONARY, n. One whose occupation is to make confections or sweetmeats.
CONFECTION, n. A composition or mixture; a sweetmeat; a preparation of fruits or juices with sugar.
APOTHECARY, n. One who practices pharmacy; one who prepares drugs and spices.
CONSCRIPTION, n. A compulsory enrolment of men for military or other service.
TYRANNY, n. Arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; oppression; cruel government.
scriptures: And he will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers.

And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots.
And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.
And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the LORD will not hear you in that day.
corruption_summary: The state is looked to as the solution to a people's insecurity, and its growth accepted as the price; 1 Samuel 8 records God's own diagnosis, that the demand for such a king was a rejection of his rule.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel's request was not for anarchy but for security and normality: make us a king to judge us like all the nations. Samuel's reply is an itemised forecast of what a state large enough to guarantee that will take, and the verbs are all seizure. Sons for the chariots, daughters for the kitchens, fields and vineyards and oliveyards, the tenth of the seed and of the flock, and finally the men themselves — ye shall be his servants. Scripture's political realism here is older and harder than any modern party's. Every guarantee is purchased with a taking.

The dictionary holds the three God-ordained spheres — family, church, and state — each with its own proper authority under Christ, and 1 Samuel 8 is the classic text on what happens when one absorbs the others. But the chapter's decisive verse is theological rather than political: they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. A people looking to a magistrate for what only God gives has already made a religious decision, whatever the ballot says, and God's answer was to grant the request. He gave them Saul.

pos: n. (a keeper of cattle; the trade Amos named when he was ordered out of Bethel)
etymology: From herd and man. The Authorized Version uses the singular once, in Amos's answer to Amaziah the priest of Bethel: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman.
biblical_def: Amaziah the priest of Bethel had just told Amos to take his preaching elsewhere: O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there. The insinuation is that the prophet is working for his supper. Amos's answer cuts the accusation off at the root: Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit. He had a trade. He had no standing in the prophetic guilds, no office, no salary, and nothing to gain from the message that was getting him expelled. What he had was a call, and the next verse states it without adornment: the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. Two verbs, both God's. Paul states the same principle for the church age: God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one employed in tending herds of cattle; in Scripture, the trade of Amos, who was taken from following the flock to prophesy.
webster_full: HERDMAN, n. One employed in tending herds of cattle.
HERD, n. A collection or assemblage of beasts, as distinguished from a flock of sheep.
SYCAMORE, n. A species of fig tree, the fruit of which grows on the trunk and large branches.
CALL, n. Divine vocation, or summons; as the call of Abraham.
COMMISSION, n. The act of committing or entrusting; a warrant or written authority.
scriptures: Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Amo 7:12
Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there:
Amo 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: A preacher's authority is located in credentials, institutional standing, or platform, so that a man without them is dismissed; Amos disclaims every credential he has and rests the whole weight on the LORD took me.
corruption_paragraphs: Amaziah's move is the oldest in the book: question the man's motives and his standing rather than answer his message. Go and eat bread somewhere else, seer. Amos does not defend his standing because he has none to defend, and that is the point of his reply. He was a herdman and a gatherer of sycomore fruit — a man who scratched the unripe figs so they would ripen, which is about as far from a religious career as the ancient world offered. The authority in his mouth was not his own and never had been.

The dictionary is not against training. The church is commanded to commit the word to faithful men who shall be able to teach others also, and the Reformed tradition has always prized a learned ministry. What it denies is that the credential is the authority. A man may have every qualification an institution can give and no word from God, and the test Scripture actually applies to a prophet is whether what he says is true and whether it turns people to the LORD. Amaziah had the office, the altar, and the king's ear, and the word came to the man with the figs.

pos: n. (the keeper of a prison; the Philippian convert of Acts 16)
etymology: From Old French gaiole, a cage, through gaoler. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the man at Philippi charged to keep Paul and Silas safely, who before morning asked them how to be saved.
biblical_def: And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely. He did his work thoroughly: the inner prison, and their feet made fast in the stocks. At midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them. The earthquake opened every door and loosed every band, and the keeper of the prison, awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, drew out his sword and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled — a Roman officer's reflex, since he would answer with his life for an escape. Paul cried with a loud voice, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here. Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas, and brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? The answer is the plainest statement of the gospel in the book of Acts: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. He washed their stripes the same hour of the night, and was baptized, he and all his, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the keeper of a jail or prison; in Scripture, the Philippian keeper who was converted the night of the earthquake.
webster_full: JAILOR, n. The keeper of a jail or prison.
PRISON, n. A house or place of confinement, particularly for debtors and criminals.
STOCKS, n. A machine consisting of two pieces of timber, in which the legs of criminals are confined.
CONVERSION, n. In a theological sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart is subdued.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family.
scriptures: And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely:
And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled.
And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
corruption_summary: The gospel is presented as a therapeutic improvement or a life-enhancement rather than a rescue from judgment; the jailor's question is What must I do to be saved, and the apostolic answer names a Person to be believed on and nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 16:30 is the question that modern presentation most often avoids and the apostles most often answered. The man does not ask how to find purpose, or how to fix his household, or how to be happier; he asks to be saved, having just been about to take his own life. And the answer given by inspiration is nine words about an object of faith: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved. Not believe about him — believe on him, resting the whole weight on a Person. Everything else in the account follows as fruit: the washing of stripes, the baptism, the meal, the rejoicing.

The promise and thy house is not a guarantee of automatic salvation for relatives, and the verse itself shows why: they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house, and the household believed and rejoiced. The word was preached to every one of them. What the promise does is hold out God's ordinary way of working through families, which is why the covenant household matters in Scripture from Noah to Cornelius. The head of the house heard, and then his whole house heard, and by morning the man who had put Paul in the stocks was washing the marks he had made.

pos: n. (one who cuts grass or grain with a scythe)
etymology: From mow, Old English mawan, to cut down grass. The Authorized Version uses it once, in a song of ascents, of the harvester whose hand is never filled by grass grown on a roof.
biblical_def: Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom. The psalm is a song of the afflicted nation: many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say; the plowers plowed upon my back, they made long their furrows. And then the prayer against those who hate Zion, and the figure this verse belongs to: let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up. Grass on a flat mud roof sprouts fast in the shallow dirt and dies in the sun before anyone could cut it, so there is nothing for the mower's hand to gather and nothing for the binder's arms. It is the picture of a life with no harvest in it — not violently destroyed, simply come to nothing. The psalm adds the loneliest detail last: neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the LORD be upon you. No passer-by gives the harvest greeting, because there is no harvest. Isaiah uses the same grass for all flesh, and puts beside it the thing that does not wither: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth, but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who mows; one who cuts grass with a scythe; in Scripture, the harvester whose hand the rooftop grass never fills.
webster_full: MOWER, n. One who mows; one who cuts grass with a scythe.
MOW, v.t. To cut down with a scythe, as grass or other plants.
SHEAF, n. A quantity of the stalks of wheat, rye, oats or barley bound together.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house; in eastern countries, flat and used as a place of resort.
BARRENNESS, n. Unfruitfulness; sterility; want of the power of conceiving or producing.
scriptures: Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom.
Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up:
Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the LORD be upon you: we bless you in the name of the LORD.
Isa 40:7
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.
corruption_summary: Visible growth is taken for fruitfulness, so that a rapid flourishing is counted as evidence of God's blessing; the psalm's rooftop grass grows fastest of all and fills no hand.
corruption_paragraphs: Rooftop grass is the psalm's image for growth without depth, and the Lord used a nearly identical picture in the parable of the sower, of seed on stony ground that sprang up immediately because it had no deepness of earth, and withered when the sun was up because it had no root. Both pictures target the same mistake: speed and greenness read as health. A ministry, a movement, or a profession of faith may come up quickly for exactly the reason it will not last, and the test Scripture applies is not the sprouting but the mower's hand at harvest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, and the principle to recover is the patience of the biblical harvest. The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it. The barren fig tree in Luke 13 got a year of digging and dunging before the question of cutting it down was settled. The blessing the passers-by withhold in Psalm 129 is the one every labourer wants to hear over his own work, and it is spoken over real sheaves.

pos: n. pl. (men appointed to bury the dead; the burial detail after Gog)
etymology: From bury, Old English byrgan, to hide or inter. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the appointed men who went through the land after the fall of Gog, burying what the passengers marked.
biblical_def: And the passengers that pass through the land, when any seeth a man's bone, then shall he set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the valley of Hamongog. Ezekiel is describing the cleansing of the land after the overthrow, and he describes it as a work detail with a procedure. Seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them, that they may cleanse the land. Men of continual employment are separated to the task; travellers who find a bone set up a marker rather than touching it; the buriers follow and inter it; the valley itself is renamed. The care is ceremonial as well as sanitary, since contact with a dead body defiled under the law, and the land itself is the thing being cleansed. What the chapter is aiming at is stated plainly at its end: I will set my glory among the heathen, and all the heathen shall see my judgment that I have executed. Scripture's honour for the dead body is rooted in the same doctrine that makes this careful: man is made in the image of God, and the body is not a discarded shell but a thing to be sown in dishonour and raised in glory.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who buries a deceased person; in Scripture, the men appointed to inter the slain of Gog and so cleanse the land.
webster_full: BURIER, n. One who buries a deceased person.
BURY, v.t. To deposit a dead body in the earth; to inter; to entomb.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
DEFILE, v.t. To make unclean; to render foul or dirty; to pollute ceremonially.
RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave.
scriptures: And the passengers that pass through the land, when any seeth a man's bone, then shall he set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the valley of Hamongog.
And seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them, that they may cleanse the land.
And also the name of the city shall be Hamonah. Thus shall they cleanse the land.
And I will set my glory among the heathen, and all the heathen shall see my judgment that I have executed, and my hand that I have laid upon them.
corruption_summary: The body is treated as a husk once the person has departed, so that its disposal becomes a matter of convenience; Scripture buries with ceremony because the body is part of the man and is destined for resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel gives seven months, a named valley, a corps of workers, and a marking system to the burial of enemy dead, and the trouble taken is itself a doctrine. Scripture is full of such trouble. Abraham bought a field to bury Sarah rather than accept it as a gift; Joseph made the children of Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt, and they did, four centuries later; Joseph of Arimathaea begged the body of Jesus and laid it in his own new tomb; devout men carried Stephen to his burial and made great lamentation over him. The body is not the discarded packaging of a soul. It is half of what a man is, and it is going to be raised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond a general carelessness, and the principle to recover is the Christian doctrine of the body. It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. That is why the church has always buried its dead with honour and hope rather than merely disposing of remains, and why the graveyard beside the meeting house was never morbid. It was a statement about what will happen there.

pos: n. pl. (in vine dressers, those who tend and prune vines)
etymology: From dress, Old French dresser, to set in order or make straight. The Authorized Version uses the plural in vine dressers, of the men Uzziah employed in the mountains and in Carmel, for he loved husbandry.
biblical_def: Also he built towers in the desert, and digged many wells: for he had much cattle, both in the low country, and in the plains: husbandmen also, and vine dressers in the mountains, and in Carmel: for he loved husbandry. The Chronicler gives Uzziah a long and admiring paragraph — towers, wells, herds, vineyards, engines invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones, and a name that spread far abroad, for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong. Then the hinge of his life, and one of the most quoted verses in Chronicles: but when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense. Eighty priests withstood him, the leprosy rose in his forehead, and he was a leper to the day of his death, dwelling in a several house. The vine dressers stand in the good half of that paragraph. God gave him the wells and the vineyards and the victories, and the very strength that came from them became the occasion of his ruin. The Lord's own use of the trade is gentler and more searching: the dresser of the vineyard who begs one more year for the barren fig tree.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who dresses; a vine dresser, one who tends and trims vines; in Scripture, the labourers Uzziah set in the mountains and in Carmel.

HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer; tillage or cultivation of the soil.
PRUNE, v.t. To lop or cut off the superfluous branches of trees, to make them bear better fruit.
HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.
scriptures: Also he built towers in the desert, and digged many wells: for he had much cattle, both in the low country, and in the plains: husbandmen also, and vine dressers in the mountains, and in Carmel: for he loved husbandry.
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.
Luk 13:7
Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?
Joh 15:1

corruption_summary: Success is treated as a stable condition rather than a season of peculiar danger; the Chronicler puts Uzziah's ruin in a single clause — when he was strong, his heart was lifted up.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 26:16 is the sentence the dictionary would hang in every prosperous church office. Uzziah did nothing wrong while he was weak. He sought God in the days of Zechariah, and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper. The danger arrived with the prosperity, and it arrived in the specific form of a man deciding that his standing entitled him to a priest's office. Strength did not corrupt him by making him wicked in the ordinary sense; it made him think the boundaries were for other people.

The priests' response is worth as much as the warning. Azariah and eighty priests that were valiant men withstood the king to his face and told him to go out of the sanctuary, and the leprosy rose while the censer was in his hand. Courage in the ministry means telling a strong man the one thing everyone around him has stopped saying. And the Lord's parable gives the other side of the trade: the dresser pleading for one more year over a barren tree, digging about it and dunging it, which is what patient pastoral labour actually looks like when the owner has every right to cut.

pos: n. pl. (men who take fish for a living; the trade of the first disciples)
etymology: From fisher and men. The Authorized Version uses this form once, in Luke's account of the call by the lake of Gennesaret, where the fishermen had gone out of their ships and were washing their nets.
biblical_def: And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets. It is the end of a night's work and a failed one. The Lord teaches the people out of Simon's ship and then gives an order that no fisherman would have expected from a carpenter: Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught. Simon's reply contains both the objection and the obedience: Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. The catch broke the net and filled two ships until they began to sink, and the effect on Simon was not delight but terror: he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord. A display of power in the one area where he was the expert told him who was in the boat. And the commission follows the confession: Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men. They brought their ships to land, forsook all, and followed him. The trade was not discarded but transposed — the same patience, the same nets, the same deep water, aimed now at men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to catch fish; in Scripture, the trade of Simon, Andrew, James and John before the call.
webster_full: FISHERMAN, n. One whose occupation is to catch fish.
NET, n. An instrument for catching fish and fowls, or wild beasts, formed with twine or thread.
DRAUGHT, n. The act of drawing a net; the quantity of fishes taken by once drawing the net.
CALL, v.t. To invite or summon; in theology, to invite to enter into the kingdom of God.
DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
scriptures: Luk 5:2
And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets.
Luk 5:4
Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
Luk 5:8
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
Luk 5:10
And so was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.
corruption_summary: Calling is spoken of as the discovery of a personal passion, when Scripture presents it as a summons from outside a man that interrupts the work he was already doing and often contradicts his expertise.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern vocabulary of vocation runs inward: find what you love, follow it, and the world's need will meet you there. Luke 5 runs the other way. Simon was doing what he loved and was good at, had just failed at it all night, and received an instruction that his professional judgment contradicted. The call comes from the Lord standing in the boat, and the word the New Testament uses for it is a summons. Amos was following a flock, Matthew was sitting at the receipt of custom, Paul was on the Damascus road doing the opposite of God's will. Not one of them found his calling; each was called.

The order of events in the chapter is also doctrine. The miracle exposes Simon to himself, the confession follows — Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord — and only then comes the commission and the promise. Conviction of sin is not a gloomy preliminary that mature Christians grow out of; it is how a man learns who is in the boat with him. And the Lord's answer to a man asking him to leave is Fear not, and a life's work.

pos: n. (the chief architect or builder; Paul's description of his own foundation-laying)
etymology: From master and builder, rendering Greek architekton, the chief craftsman. The Authorized Version uses it once, where Paul describes his own work at Corinth as laying a foundation on which others build.
biblical_def: According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. Paul is addressing a church dividing into parties around teachers — I am of Paul, I of Apollos — and his answer is a building site with one owner. He is a labourer together with God, the Corinthians are God's husbandry and God's building, and even the skill he exercises is according to the grace of God which is given unto me. The foundation is then named and the naming forecloses every alternative: for other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. What follows is the sobering half. Men build on that foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, and every man's work shall be made manifest, for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire, and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. A man's work may burn and the man be saved, yet so as by fire. Ministry is inspected, and the inspection is by fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the chief or principal builder; an architect; in Scripture, Paul's description of his own foundation-laying at Corinth.
webster_full: MASTER-BUILDER, n. The chief builder; an architect.
ARCHITECT, n. A person skilled in the art of building; one who understands architecture.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of anything; that on which anything stands.
EDIFY, v.t. To build, in a moral and religious sense; to instruct and improve the mind in knowledge.
STUBBLE, n. The stumps of wheat, rye, barley, oats or buckwheat, left in the ground.
scriptures: According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is.
corruption_summary: Ministry is evaluated by visible results, so that size and momentum are read as gold; Paul says the day will declare it and that the test is fire, which will burn wood, hay and stubble whatever they looked like when built.
corruption_paragraphs: The Corinthian church had teachers with followings, and Paul's reply is to make the whole enterprise God's. Neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. The labourers are labourers together with God, and even the wisdom of the masterbuilder is grace given. Every measure of ministry that begins with the man rather than the owner is reading the site plan upside down, and the Corinthian parties were the first-century form of a very modern habit.

The fire is what keeps this from becoming complacency. Every man's work shall be made manifest; the day shall declare it; the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. Gold and stubble look different only under heat, and much of what is built on the true foundation with genuine sincerity will not survive the inspection. That is not a threat against salvation — he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire — but it is a serious word to anyone who builds. And the foundation itself is never in question, which is the comfort underneath the warning: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
